blocks.md: Take the growth model from earlier in the course — households choosing how much to consume and save over an infinite horizon, firms combining capital and labor — and add one thing: productivity is hit by random shocks. In a good year, workers are more productive, so households work more and invest more; in a bad year, the reverse. Recessions are then not failures of markets but the best response to temporarily bad technology. This was the first dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model: dynamic, with random shocks, and with every market clearing. It matched the ups and downs of output, hours and investment surprisingly well, which raised the question of whether it was too good to be true.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It established the method — optimizing agents, rational expectations, calibration — that all modern macro models, including New Keynesian ones, use.

(The equations are beyond the lecture, which describes the model in words.) Households maximize $E_0\sum_t \beta^t u(c_t, l_t)$; firms produce $y_t = A_t f(k_t, h_t)$; capital accumulates $k_{t+1} = (1-\delta)k_t + i_t$; and log TFP follows an AR(1),
All markets clear and prices are flexible. The model is solved for its stochastic equilibrium and simulated; simulated moments are compared with [HP-filtered](note:hodrick-prescott-filter) data.

blocks.md:
- **What are the shocks?** Measured TFP is the [Solow Residual](note:solow-residual): anything not in capital or labor, possibly "animal spirits".
- **Filtered data only.** The fit is to deviations from an HP trend; on unfiltered data and without measured TFP the model tracks the data poorly.
- **Unsatisfying assumptions:** exogenous TFP, competitive markets and flexible prices, Cobb-Douglas production, no useful role for policy, a representative agent. Each motivated a later development: [Endogenous Growth Models](note:endogenous-growth-models), the [New Keynesian Model](note:new-keynesian-model), heterogeneous-agent models.

blocks.md:
- **Thinking "real" means adjusted for inflation.** It means the shocks are real (technology), not monetary.
- **Calling every DSGE model an RBC model.** New Keynesian models are DSGE models too, with sticky prices and policy.
- Macroeconomics: the core of DSGE modeling; calibration; the benchmark for business-cycle facts.
